Three questions: data and evidence design

Malaria is a leading preventable cause of death in young children, and ITNs are the main prevention tool. This dashboard asks three different questions. An answer to one does not answer the others.

Source audit of the original 63-country table

The audited fields are national ITN use, the poorest and richest quintile values, the derived wealth gap and under-five mortality. Each was compared with the official snapshot. Region and survey year are kept as recorded in the original table, and the income group is the FY2024 classification, not a certified historical one. Legacy values are kept beside the adopted ones; nothing is overwritten. “Equal” means the value agrees with the snapshot. It does not prove which survey the original table was compiled from: that table records no survey ID.

Mortality: legacy value vs WDI snapshot

Differences above 1.5 per 1,000 live births. The cause is not established (estimate vintage or reference year), so the legacy value is kept only in the historical baseline.

Data layers, exposures and indicator definitions

Read before interpreting

  • Different exposures. The cross-section uses the share of children under five who slept under an ITN (household surveys). The annual panel uses modelled whole-population ITN use. Their coefficients are not comparable.
  • Mixed years. The cross-section has one survey per country, from . It is not a same-year comparison.
  • Outcome is all-cause. Under-five mortality (per 1,000 live births, UN IGME) includes many causes that nets cannot affect, and is itself a smoothed model estimate.
  • MAP values are model estimates. Bounds are shown as “source bounds”; their level is not documented in this snapshot. All three ITN series for 2024 repeat 2023, so the panel stops at 2023.
  • Income group is the classification stored in the original table (FY2024 thresholds), not the group in the survey year. A continuous alternative (GDP per capita, PPP) is used as a sensitivity check.

Group differences behind the raw sign

In this sample, Sub-Saharan African and low-income countries have both higher ITN use and higher mortality. One possible explanation is that higher-risk settings also receive more ITN programmes; this analysis does not establish that mechanism.

Two comparisons.
Two primary estimates.

Relative difference in under-five mortality per +10 percentage points of ITN use. This is a ratio of mortality rates, not a change in percentage points. The two estimates use different exposures and different comparisons, so they are drawn on separate axes and are not two measurements of one quantity.

Primary cross-section model: formula and coefficients

Region enters as one indicator (Sub-Saharan Africa) and income as one indicator (low income). This is not a full six-region, four-income-group adjustment and does not remove all geographic or economic confounding. With every category as its own dummy, the single high-income country gets leverage and robust standard errors become unstable, so that coding is not used.

Does ITN add
predictive information?

Choose a validation scenario first. Compare learners only when their inputs match, within the same validation scenario. These comparisons are exploratory; no learner is declared the winner.

Sample, inputs and nested validation

Two different questions are checked. New country: all data of a country are held out, so the model has never seen it. Later years: the countries are known and only their later years are held out. Choose a validation scenario first; it fixes the sample and the validation scheme. In the “same features” and annual-panel scenarios every learner also receives the same inputs, so learners can be compared with each other. In the “as first reported” scenarios the two learners were given different encodings, so only the comparison without and with ITN inside one learner is valid. Scores from different scenarios are never ranked together.

How the validation was run

    Research,
    at a glance.

    Question

    Do countries where more children sleep under insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) have lower under-five mortality, who is covered, and does ITN use add information to a prediction of mortality?

    Three results

    My contribution

    In the original three-person course project, I was responsible for the introduction, narrative and world map. For the later re-analysis, I supplied written specifications and review notes.

    The evidence,
    and its limits.

    Coverage varies by wealth; the adjusted association remains uncertain; ITN adds no clear predictive improvement in these checks. These country-level, all-cause mortality data do not estimate protection for individual net users. The sensitivity calculation on the Adjusted models page explains what this design could detect.

    These data support

    • A description of coverage: levels and gaps by country, year and wealth quintile.
    • A country-level adjusted association with its interval: close to zero, direction not determined.
    • A prediction check: in these models and validation schemes, adding ITN gave no clear reduction in held-out error.

    They do not support

    • Whether nets protect the children who use them. No individual-level or causal effect is estimated.
    • “No effect”. Intervals that include zero do not show absence of effect or equivalence.
    • A statement about malaria deaths. The outcome is all-cause under-five mortality.
    • A forecast. The later-years check uses observed covariates of the test years.

          Research decisions

          Three decisions that changed the project: the question, the evidence, and what was decided. The numbers are read from the current analysis output.

          1. Repair the source table. Adopt official-source values and keep the legacy baseline.
          2. Hold out whole countries and later years. Match validation to the prediction question.
          3. Report every configuration. Keep simple baselines and paired error changes visible.
          Evidence behind the three decisions
          All five decisions in full
            Findings that changed the original story

            Null results and models that did worse than a simple baseline stay on the page with their numbers.

              What changed from v2.1
              Full limitations: design, sources and validation
              • Ecological design. Country averages cannot describe what happens to individual children.
              • Confounding by malaria risk. Transmission intensity may confound the association: it can be related to both ITN programmes and mortality. This analysis does not identify the allocation mechanism, and region or country effects may leave residual confounding.
              • All-cause, model-based outcome. Under-five mortality is an estimated UN IGME series and the panel shows serial dependence, so country-years cannot be treated as independent observations.
              • Modelled exposure in the panel. MAP ITN use is an estimate; its uncertainty is not propagated into the regressions.
              • Survey identity. DHS surveys are matched by country, year and value. A match shows consistency with that survey, not that the original table was compiled from it.
              • Conditional retrospective validation. The future-year check uses the observed covariates and ITN values of the test years, from the latest revised series. It is not a forecast that could have been made at the time.
              • Model set. The models and lags shown are one fixed set reported in full. They were not pre-registered.
              • Quintile sources. of 63 legacy quintile pairs could not be matched to a survey in the package and stay labelled unverified.
              • No gap intervals. A confidence interval for a Q5 − Q1 gap needs the survey microdata.

              Next step: move below national averages

              Apply for DHS survey microdata to study child-level outcomes with survey weights, clusters and strata. This is future work.

              Methods and reproduction commands

              Methods in brief

              • Source audit: comparison of national ITN use, quintile values, the wealth gap and mortality in the legacy table with the official snapshot (tab 1).
              • Equity: five wealth quintiles for six DHS indicators (tab 2).
              • Association: log-linear regression with HC3 errors; two-way fixed effects with country-clustered t intervals (a wild-cluster bootstrap gives a p-value as a sensitivity check); Bayesian partial pooling with diagnostics (tabs 3 and 4).
              • Prediction: leave-one-country-out and rolling-origin validation; baselines, Ridge and random forests; nested tuning; paired error differences (tab 5).

              Reproduction

              • Run python3 pipeline/run_all.py in the delivered package: raw snapshot → curated tables → analysis → results → this page. The full run takes more than an hour on two CPU cores; most of it is the nested tuning.
              • Current release checks: python3 checks/verify_release.py. Scientific checks with the model dependencies: python3 checks/verify_results.py. Compare retained scientific outputs with the saved baseline: python3 checks/compare_runs.py. Browser suite: node checks/acceptance.mjs. A saved-output comparison alone is not a new full-analysis reproduction.
              • The code and data are delivered as a zip package together with this page. No public repository is linked.
